shows.title: SPACE IS THE PLACE: Selections from the Hammer Contemporary Collection
shows.description:
Borrowing its title from Sun Ra's 1973 album and 1974 film, this Hammer Contemporary Collection survey turns "space" into a wide-open curatorial question. Rather than a single thesis, the show works through a constellation of ideas — Afrofuturism, migration, domestic space, and the simple, radical act of taking up room in the world — using nearly thirty artists drawn entirely from the museum's own holdings. It's a smart way to make an encyclopedic collection feel like a pointed argument.

The range of material is the pleasure here: Arthur Jafa's charged image-work sits near Betye Saar's assemblage and Fred Eversley's polished resin lenses, while younger voices like Lauren Halsey, Juliana Huxtable, and Danielle Dean push the same questions of belonging and placemaking into sculpture, photography, and video. Thomas J Price's monumental bronze of a Black woman glancing at her phone anchors one gallery with a quiet, outsized authority, and Cauleen Smith's moving-image work threads a more lyrical, essayistic register through the show.

Because this is a free-admission museum presentation rather than a commercial gallery show, there's room to wander and let the connections accumulate — between Nayland Blake's early assemblage and Rodney McMillian's material politics, between Michael Queenland's tiled wall pieces and Arcmanoro Niles's saturated interiors. It's a strong, generous survey of how Los Angeles-connected artists have used the museum's collection to think about space as both a physical and political condition, and a good reminder of how deep the Hammer's contemporary holdings actually run.

shows.title: Fragmented Thought
shows.description:
Carole Vanderlinden has spent decades making paintings that refuse to settle into one style, and this show — her latest body of oil paintings made over the past three years — is a good introduction to why that refusal is the point. Shapes drift between figuration and abstraction, surfaces build up in visible, almost sedimentary layers, and passages that look like collage are actually painted illusions of collage. The overall effect is of a mind thinking out loud on canvas, doubling back on itself and letting contradictory ideas sit side by side.

The Belgian painter's reference points are eclectic and mostly submerged — early modernists like Malevich and Picabia, her own sketchbooks, stray bits of art history — but none of it surfaces as direct quotation. What comes through instead is a sustained interest in the gap between form and content, in how a mark can carry meaning without illustrating anything in particular. It's an intellectually restless kind of painting that rewards slow looking rather than quick reads.

This is Vanderlinden's second solo outing with Karma's Los Angeles space, and it arrives alongside the artist's first monograph. For anyone interested in painting that treats its own materials and history as raw subject matter, rather than in service of a tidy image, this is a worthwhile stop on Santa Monica Boulevard.

shows.title: All Signs Fail
shows.description:
Patrick Jackson has built a career out of taking familiar objects and images and pushing them slightly out of register, and this installation is one of his most ambitious stagings of that idea. The centerpiece is a reprint of an "Eye Syphilis Is Serious" public-health billboard that once hung around Los Angeles, blown up to 44 feet wide and stripped of its text, so that the image's original urgency curdles into something more ambiguous and unsettling. Standing in front of it are two purchased figures — an adult companion doll dressed in a hand-knitted sweater and a "reborn" baby doll — a mother-and-child tableau assembled entirely from objects made for other purposes.

Ringing the gallery walls is a run of found bus-shelter posters for remakes, sequels, and franchise films, arranged by release date and marked with screenprinted seasonal motifs — leaves, snow, flame — as if tracking the passage of time through recycled culture. Behind the billboard, a two-story scaffold structure conceals a small, maze-like memorial building visitors can walk through, turning the whole installation into something between an advertisement, a shrine, and a stage set.

Jackson, a Los Angeles-born sculptor who's shown at the Hammer and the Huntington, has described the show simply as "a lot of images and a memorial," and that plain description undersells how strange and effective the piece is in person. It's a show about how mass-produced images of care, warning, and grief circulate and lose their charge — and about what happens when an artist reassembles that debris into something that feels, unexpectedly, like a monument.

shows.title: tierra
shows.artist: Jackie Amézquita, Natalia Arbelaez, Syd Carpenter, Teresa Castro, Armando Guadalupe Cortés, rafa esparza, Miguel Fernández de Castro, Adebunmi Gbadebo, Karla García, Christine Howard Sandoval, Joanna Keane Lopez, Ruben Olguin, Iman Person, Jeri Redcorn (group exhibition)
shows.description:
tierra is the latest edition of Craft Contemporary's long-running Clay Biennial, reimagined to move past ceramics alone and take in the whole family of earth-based materials — adobe, soil, ash, clay slip, pigment made from land itself. Fourteen Latinx, Indigenous, and Black artists treat dirt and clay not as inert stuff to be shaped but as a living relative: something that remembers touch, labor, displacement, and repair. Joanna Keane Lopez's adobe wall reliefs, rafa esparza's earthen brickwork, and Jeri Redcorn's Caddo-tradition pottery sit alongside newer voices like Miguel Fernández de Castro and Adebunmi Gbadebo, whose material choices carry specific histories of land and labor in the Americas.

What makes the show more than a survey of medium is its insistence on land as archive. Pieces move between grief and stewardship — colonial extraction and border violence acknowledged alongside Indigenous frameworks of care and continuity. The curatorial team, led by Andres Payan Estrada with a committee that includes artist Cannupa Hanska Luger, frames the exhibition as a set of overlapping definitions of the Spanish word tierra: ground, homeland, sediment, ancestor.

For a museum devoted to craft, this is an ambitious swing — using a biennial historically tied to ceramics to ask bigger questions about who gets to claim land and memory through material. It's a worthwhile stop on Museum Row for anyone interested in how contemporary artists are reworking traditional and vernacular techniques into pointed, personal statements about place.

shows.title: Circle House
shows.description:
Oscar Tuazon has spent his career testing the line between sculpture and shelter, and Circle House is one of his most literal experiments yet: a inhabitable structure built from cardboard, wood, and tatami mats, organized around three circles that nod to the enso, the single-brush Zen symbol for emptiness and discipline. True to Tuazon's practice, the joinery and structural logic are left exposed rather than hidden — you can see exactly how the thing holds itself up.

The piece extends ideas Tuazon has explored for years about building as both a functional and a philosophical act: what does it mean to make a room, and who gets to occupy it. Staged as a long-running installation in Morán Morán's Western Avenue space, it gives visitors an unusually long window — nearly the whole year — to sit with a work that's as much architecture as it is object.

For anyone interested in the intersection of sculpture, self-built structures, and contemplative practice, this is a low-key must-see, and its extended run means there's no need to rush.

shows.title: The Expanding Field: MOCA's Collection from the 1940s to 1970s
shows.description:
MOCA turns to its own holdings for this survey, using the postwar decades as a case study in how contemporary art actually got that way. Rather than a tidy march from Abstract Expressionism to Pop to Minimalism, the show leans into the tangle of movements that competed and overlapped in the 1940s through 70s, pulling together painting, sculpture, and assemblage from the museum's deep permanent collection.

It's the kind of show that rewards close looking rather than a quick lap: expect the density of a collection exhibition, with lesser-shown works from the vault set alongside the postwar heavyweights MOCA is known for. For a museum literally founded to steward this era of art, this is as close to a mission statement as it gets, and a good primer for anyone trying to understand how Los Angeles's own postwar scene fit into the larger story.

As a collection show drawing entirely from MOCA's holdings, it's a good complement to more thematic, single-artist exhibitions elsewhere in the building, and free admission days make it an easy add to a Downtown museum visit before it closes in late September.

shows.title: Yoko Ono: Music of the Mind
shows.description:
Yoko Ono's first solo museum survey in Southern California treats her not as John Lennon's collaborator but as the conceptual artist she was well before the Beatles ever met her: a key figure in Fluxus whose instruction pieces, films, and participatory works helped invent the idea that an artwork could be something a visitor completes rather than just looks at. The Broad's presentation spans seven decades, from spare 1960s text works to the immersive, hands-on installations she's best known for today.

That participatory streak is the heart of the show. Visitors are invited to tie a wish to an olive tree, hammer a nail into a painting, write a note to their mother and pin it to a wall, or add a stroke of blue marker to a boat-shaped sculpture representing displacement and refuge. Alongside these interactive works are historical touchstones like "Cut Piece" and "Fly," which show Ono working through vulnerability, gender, and the body decades before those became gallery-standard subjects.

It's a rare chance to see Ono treated with full institutional weight rather than as a footnote to rock history, and the hands-on nature of the work makes it one of the more genuinely fun, all-ages museum visits in the city right now. General admission at The Broad is free, though the special exhibition requires a timed ticket.

shows.title: Presence
shows.description:
Havana-based Roberto Diago makes his West Coast debut with a suite of mixed-media portraits and still lifes built from reclaimed wood, nails, cord, and canvas. The portraits are deliberately withholding: faces reduced to a pair of eyes, a beaded necklace, a wedge of shadow, set into grids of scavenged material that fracture the picture plane the way early modernist collage once did. The still lifes strip a vase and a few flowers down to flat, graphic silhouettes against saturated color.

Diago has spent three decades using found materials from his Havana neighborhood to talk about the afterlives of racism in Cuban society, and the rawness of his materials, splintered wood, exposed nails, is the point rather than a stylistic flourish. The grid structures running through many of these works read as a visual metaphor for the divisions imposed on Afro-Cuban communities, with the scavenged materials pointing to both scarcity and resilience.

This show arrives while Diago is also representing Cuba at the Venice Biennale, and it's a good introduction to an artist who's had a substantial institutional exhibition history in the U.S. (the Halsey Institute, the Art Museum of the Americas) but comparatively little gallery exposure in Los Angeles until now.

shows.title: The Hunter
shows.description:
Daido Moriyama's first major Los Angeles exhibition gathers decades of the grainy, high-contrast street photography that made him one of the defining figures of postwar Japanese image-making. Associated with the radical Provoke movement, Moriyama built a visual language out of what most photographers try to eliminate — blur, grain, and loss of focus, known in Japanese as are-bure-boke — treating the camera less as a recording device than as an extension of his own restless movement through the city.

The images here are fragments rather than scenes: a stray dog's eyes, a passing gesture, a flash of signage, a body glimpsed and gone. Moriyama has always insisted he wasn't going out to photograph life so much as to experience it, camera in hand, and that sense of pursuit — of the hunter chasing something that won't hold still — gives the show its title.

For a photographer this influential to still feel dangerous and unresolved on the wall says something about how good the prints are. It's a compact but intense survey, well worth the trip out to Bergamot Station.

shows.title: Private Show
shows.description:
Long before his Weimaraners made him a household name, William Wegman was one of the sharpest conceptual photographers to come out of 1970s Los Angeles, and this show digs into that formative decade with rare vintage prints and video alongside later work that shows where those early ideas ended up. After relocating to Southern California in 1970, Wegman fell in with Ed Ruscha, John Baldessari, and Allen Ruppersberg, and his photography grew directly out of performance — deadpan visual jokes that double as small philosophical experiments about looking and language.

Pieces like A Basic Guide to Lettering literally flip an instructional format on its head, while later Polaroids featuring his dogs — Eye On, Trio of One — bring the same absurdist precision to a completely different scale and subject. Seeing the two eras side by side makes clear how consistent Wegman's wit has been across fifty years, even as the tools and subjects changed.

It's a smart, funny, image-rich show from an artist people tend to underrate precisely because he's so good at being funny.

shows.title: Marilyn Monroe: Hollywood Icon
shows.description:
Timed to what would have been Marilyn Monroe's hundredth birthday, this sprawling Rolex Gallery exhibition treats her less as a tragic icon than as a working actor who understood image-making as craft. Hundreds of objects — contact sheets, studio memos, fan mail, wardrobe tests, and personal letters, many shown for the first time — trace how a contract player born Norma Jeane Mortenson built and controlled "Marilyn Monroe" inside a studio system designed to own her image outright.

The costume holdings are the showstoppers: Orry-Kelly's gowns from Some Like It Hot, the unmistakable pink Travilla number from Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, and pieces from the unfinished Something's Got to Give, staged in dramatic vitrines that read as much like couture display as film history. Curator Sophia Serrano uses the wardrobe and paperwork together to make an argument: Monroe's glamour was labor, negotiated scene by scene, dress fitting by dress fitting.

For a museum built around the mechanics of moviemaking, it's a smart fit — less a celebrity shrine than a case study in how a studio-era star authored her own myth. Given the costumes and ephemera on loan, this is very much a look-but-don't-touch show, and worth the wait in line on a busy Wilshire Boulevard weekend.

shows.title: Now We're There (And We' Only Just Begun)
shows.description:
This single-painting installation inaugurates LACMA's new W.M. Keck Foundation Gallery, a space the museum has dedicated to sustained encounters with individual works by contemporary artists. The painting itself, recently acquired by the museum, is vintage Quarles: bodies stretch, double back, and dissolve into one another across a hot, patterned field, the artist's signature warping of line and color making it hard to tell where one figure ends and another begins.

Quarles, who lives and works in Los Angeles, has spent the last decade building a reputation as one of the most inventive painters of the body working today, and this acquisition-and-solo-showcase model gives Angelenos a rare chance to sit with a single major canvas rather than breeze past it in a crowded group show. The tangled, ambiguous figures speak to her long-running interest in mixed-race, queer identity and the slipperiness of being seen and categorized by others.

It's a small show in footprint but a significant one institutionally, marking the start of an ongoing series at LACMA built around deep dives into one artist's work. Free with museum admission, it's worth pairing with the encyclopedic collection just steps away.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: Cordillera Mexicana: Alfredo Ramos Martínez and the Mexican Landscape
shows.description:
Alfredo Ramos Martínez is often called the father of Mexican Modernism — he mentored David Alfaro Siqueiros and Rufino Tamayo and pushed a generation of painters out of the studio and into the landscape. This exhibition, drawn from the artist's estate (which Louis Stern Fine Arts exclusively represents), gathers tempera-on-paper and oil landscapes made after his 1929 move to Los Angeles, when homesickness for Mexico's mountains and markets became a lifelong subject.

The show's anchor works trace a single mental thread: the Cordillera, the mountain spine that runs from the Sierra Madre down through the Americas. Martínez's Cordillera Mexicana pays tribute to the Sierra Madre Oriental peaks above his native Monterrey, while other paintings place indigenous women bearing flowers and produce beneath the volcanoes ringing the Valley of Mexico. Even his delicate studies of floripondio blossoms — a South American flower he found growing as an ornamental in both Mexico and Southern California — read as a metaphor for his own transplanted life.

It's a quieter, more historical show than most of what's on view in LA's contemporary-leaning galleries right now, but a good one for anyone curious about the roots of Mexican modernism as seen from Los Angeles, a city where Martínez spent his final two decades and where his legacy is held in depth at LACMA and beyond.

shows.title: Object Poetry
shows.description:
"Object Poetry" gathers artists who treat sculpture and assemblage as a kind of compressed language, where everyday materials and cast-off objects are recombined until they start to read like verse. The checklist spans generations and temperaments: Bruce Conner's uncanny assemblage sensibility sits alongside Tony Oursler's video-inflected sculptures, large-scale photographic works, and pieces that play with domestic scale and architectural miniature. Across the two galleries, the through-line is a fascination with objecthood itself — the way a chair leg, a lens, or a scrap of fabric can carry more meaning once it's pulled out of use and set into a composition.

Michael Kohn Gallery has spent four decades building relationships with exactly this kind of artist — people who use assemblage, collage, and sculptural accumulation to talk about memory, media, and the residue of everyday life. Seeing the works installed together across the gallery's two main rooms makes clear how much these different practices share: a belief that objects, arranged with enough attention, behave like sentences.

This is a good show for anyone who likes sculpture that rewards close looking — pieces built from many small decisions rather than one big gesture. It's on view concurrently with a solo survey of Mark Innerst's paintings in the gallery's third room, making a visit worth the time for two very different but complementary shows under one roof.

shows.title: You want to hear echoes
shows.description:
Leo Mock's paintings read like fragments of overheard conversation — each one titled with a wistful, slightly melancholic phrase ("The stars have grown old," "Pull the smiles inside," "We can pretend we're that") that sets up a small emotional scene before you've even looked at the paint. The works themselves are moody, layered figurative compositions, built up with a loose, expressive hand that leaves plenty of drips, scrapes, and second thoughts visible on the surface.

Presented at M+B's Casa MB space, an intimate, house-like extension of the gallery's main Almont Drive location, the show benefits from close, room-scaled viewing. Mock's palette tends toward bruised blues and warm ochres, and figures often seem to be dissolving into or emerging from their backgrounds, which suits the show's overall tone of longing and half-remembered feeling.

It's a quiet, literary kind of painting show — good for anyone who likes work that rewards spending real time with the titles as well as the images. The exhibition closes September 5, so this is very much a last-chance viewing before it comes down.

shows.title: Odilon Redon: Otherworldly Visions
shows.description:
Odilon Redon spent the late nineteenth century turning charcoal and lithographic crayon into a private mythology of eyeballs adrift in black skies, cyclopean monsters, and flowers that seem to breathe. This exhibition, drawn substantially from the Getty's own holdings, gathers the artist's noirs — those velvety charcoal drawings that first made his reputation in Symbolist Paris — alongside the lithograph albums and jewel-toned pastels of his later years.

What makes Redon such a satisfying subject for a collection show is the hinge his career represents: trained in the shadow of academic history painting, he pushed toward something closer to the unconscious, anticipating Surrealism decades before the term existed. The Getty's presentation leans into that darkness-to-light arc, tracing how a artist obsessed with disquiet gradually let color and botanical wonder back into his work without ever losing his taste for the uncanny.

It's a quieter, more contemplative counterpart to the blockbuster photography and design shows the Getty has mounted this year, and a good excuse to spend an afternoon with works on paper that reward close, unhurried looking. Free admission, as always, and the show closes mid-October.

shows.title: The Sound of Gordon Parks
shows.description:
Everyone knows Gordon Parks the photographer — the FSA images, the Life magazine essays, "American Gothic" with Ella Watson posed in front of a flag. Fewer people know that Parks composed music for most of his adult life, writing piano concertos and film scores with the same fluency he brought to a camera. CAAM's exhibition, built with the Gordon Parks Foundation and Parks's longtime musical collaborator Mario Sprouse, is the rare show that treats that second career as a subject in its own right rather than a footnote.

Expect an immersive mix of recordings, video, and archival material — sheet music, correspondence, session photographs — that reframes Parks's visual work as part of a single, continuous creative practice rather than a separate hobby. It's a smart curatorial move for an artist whose photographs are so iconic they can overshadow everything else he made.

For a museum whose galleries sit just off the Coliseum in Exposition Park, this is exactly the kind of deep-cut biographical show that rewards the trip: intimate, well-researched, and focused on an artist whose reputation could easily fill a much shallower exhibition.

shows.title: Life, Liberty, and Los Angeles
shows.description:
The Autry has always been more interesting than its cowboy-museum reputation suggests, and this sprawling group show is a good example of why. Timed loosely around the country's semiquincentennial, "Life, Liberty, and Los Angeles" uses the city itself — its car culture, its immigrant neighborhoods, its protest history, its endless self-mythologizing — as a lens for asking what American ideals have actually meant on the ground in Southern California.

The exhibition pulls from the Autry's deep Western-history holdings as well as contemporary commissions, mixing archival photography, painted ephemera, and new work by living artists. A vintage car painted with a heart on its roof, floating over a faded map of the LA basin, sets the tone: nostalgic and a little skeptical at once, romantic about place without being uncritical about history.

It's a show built for a long run — on view into January — and worth pairing with a walk through the Autry's permanent Western galleries, which increasingly read as a running argument with this special exhibition about whose stories get remembered.

venue.name: Autry Museum of the American West

shows.title: Outsiders, Outcasts, Rebels + Weirdos: Punk Culture 1976–86
shows.description:
It's a little disorienting to find safety pins and Xeroxed flyers in a museum best known for its Jewish ceremonial art collection, and that's precisely the point. The Skirball's punk survey traces the decade between 1976 and 1986 through gig posters, stage-worn clothing, zines, and photography, with particular attention to the Jewish musicians, promoters, and scene-builders who shaped Los Angeles punk from the inside — a history that rarely gets its due next to the CBGB-centric New York narrative.

The show leans into ephemera over relics: hand-lettered flyers for shows at the Masque and the Whisky, cut-and-paste zine pages, and the visual language of a subculture that treated the photocopier as its primary printing press. Cliff Roman of the Germs and other LA scene veterans figure into the accompanying programming.

Paired with the concurrent comic-book survey down the hall, it makes for an unexpectedly countercultural season at a campus better known for Noah's Ark installations and Passover programming — proof that the Skirball's curators are willing to get a little scrappy.

shows.title: 20th Anniversary Group Show
shows.description:
Corey Helford has spent two decades building one of the country's most reliable homes for New Contemporary art — the pop-culture-inflected, technically virtuosic, narrative-driven painting and sculpture that mainstream galleries were slow to take seriously. This anniversary show, the first of a two-part celebration, gathers new work by artists who defined the gallery's program across those twenty years, from hyper-detailed figurative painters to the sculptors and muralists who've made CHG's three-gallery Downtown space a destination beyond the traditional art-world circuit.

What's notable about Corey Helford's roster is how much genuine range sits under the "lowbrow" or "pop surrealist" label: airbrush-smooth portraiture next to gothic fantasy, cartoon-adjacent character work next to fairly serious formal painting. An anniversary show like this functions as a group portrait of that range, with each artist contributing new pieces rather than simply pulling from inventory.

A second edition opens in September, so this first round is really the opening act of a longer celebration — a good excuse to see how a gallery built entirely outside the blue-chip system has quietly become an institution of its own.

shows.title: Kiddos
shows.description:
Matthew Grabelsky is best known for dropping wide-eyed animal-headed figures — his signature mash-up of human bodies and cartoon or animal faces — into the fluorescent-lit purgatory of the New York subway. "Kiddos" narrows that lens to childhood: playground scuffles, temper tantrums, sibling rivalries, and the small dramas of growing up, all rendered with the same uncanny, hyper-real polish he brings to his transit paintings.

The effect is somewhere between Norman Rockwell and a fever dream — technically dazzling figurative painting that uses its animal-headed cast to sidestep easy sentimentality about childhood. A kid mid-tantrum or a "cool kid" in a playground standoff reads as funnier and stranger with a fox or rabbit head than it would with an ordinary human face, and Grabelsky clearly knows it.

Thinkspace has spent two decades championing exactly this kind of pop-surrealist, illustration-adjacent painting, and Grabelsky's meticulous, faintly melancholic style is a good fit for a gallery that treats craft and narrative as virtues rather than liabilities.

shows.title: Yes and LA Dust
shows.description:
Thirteen years after Urs Fischer turned MOCA's galleries into a communal clay-sculpting studio, Jeffrey Deitch brings that project's afterlife home in two simultaneous shows. At the Orange Drive space, nineteen of the bronze casts pulled from that 2013 public happening stand together as a strange, democratic forest of figures — some clearly the work of a trained sculptor, others with the lumpy, sincere energy of a stranger's first attempt at clay. Fischer selected and cast them himself, and the result reads less like a survey of "good" sculpture than a group portrait of collective imagination under one artist's editorial eye.

A short walk away at the Santa Monica Boulevard gallery, the mood shifts entirely. LA Dust revives a body of work Fischer began in 2007: paintings on metal panel made from scanned dust swept off his studio floor, blown up and rendered in mirror-like, reflective surfaces that shift color depending on where you stand. Installed on the diagonal to suggest a passage from day into night, the panels turn something as inconsequential as floor grime into an argument about scale — the show's underlying idea being that dust sits in a kind of mesoscopic no-man's-land between what we can see and what we can't.

Taken together, the two venues make the case for Fischer as one of the few artists moving fluently between monumental sculpture and quiet, optical painting, and the show's Los Angeles setting is not incidental — Fischer has lived and worked in the city on and off since 2001, and both projects trace directly back to his history with this city's museums and streets. It's a rare chance to see a blue-chip artist's studio-scale ambition laid out across two full galleries at once.

shows.title: Joel-Peter Witkin: Selected Works 1974–2018
shows.description:
Joel-Peter Witkin has spent five decades building elaborately staged photographs that look like they were unearthed from some forgotten wing of art history — tableaux populated by cadavers, amputees, hermaphrodites, and other figures excluded from conventional pictures of beauty, arranged with the same compositional seriousness Velázquez or Goya brought to a royal court. This survey, pulling together prints from 1974 through 2018, traces how consistent that vision has been: the theatrical backdrops, the scratched and toned negatives, the constant citation of old-master painting even as the subject matter refuses every one of its comforts.

What makes the work more than shock value is the craft underneath it. Witkin doesn't just photograph his tableaux — he attacks the negative and print afterward, scratching the emulsion, bleaching sections, sometimes drawing directly on the surface, so that each finished piece sits somewhere between photograph and hand-worked object. The pictures reference Picasso, Courbet, and Christian iconography as often as they reference the darkroom, and the effect is a body of work that treats mortality and the marginalized body as subjects worthy of the grandest possible visual language.

Fahey/Klein has spent nearly forty years as one of the country's foremost photography galleries, and this show is a fitting anniversary gesture: a chance to see a genuinely singular, still-controversial photographic practice presented with the scholarly care usually reserved for painting retrospectives.

shows.title: Graven Images to the Major Deities
shows.description:
John Collins is best known around Los Angeles for Moonlight Graham, a daily devotional practice he's kept up since 2019: every night during baseball season, he picks a play from that day's games and renders it in brushwork and ink wash before posting it online. The series now numbers over a thousand works, and this show — Collins's second dedicated to the project at Track 16 — catches it mid-evolution, as he's swapped his original Arches paper for Asian rice and mulberry bark stock that makes the marks looser and more immediate, and ventured into drypoint printmaking for the first time with a set of prints depicting the final games of the 2025 World Series.

The project's charm is in its stubborn earnestness: Collins named the series after Archibald "Moonlight" Graham, the real-life ballplayer immortalized in Shoeless Joe and Field of Dreams who moonlighted as a doctor, and he treats his own nightly ritual — sketching after a day spent working as a handyman — as a similarly quixotic double life. Baseball, for Collins, isn't a subject so much as a structure for daily discipline, a deadline he sets for himself as if filing to tomorrow's sports section.

Outside the baseball works, Collins is known for brooding, autobiographical paintings on scavenged materials — linoleum scraps, chunks of stucco, torn fabric — that read as private ruminations rather than public statements. Seeing both bodies of work together at Track 16, in the gallery's Bendix Building space downtown, makes the case for an artist whose sincerity and repetition are the whole point.

shows.title: New Skies
shows.description:
Severin Hallauer's first Los Angeles solo show builds an entire vocabulary around inheritance — the things, memories, and even traumas we're handed before we have any say in the matter. The Mexico City-based Swiss artist works across sculpture, installation, video, and text, and the pieces here range from intimate to genuinely startling: a modified airline carry-on reworked with cut-paper patterns drawn from Swiss papercutting tradition; a single-frame video confronting a childhood memory involving a gun; and a wall of 355 stained-glass microscope slides, each one tracing a branch of Hallauer's family tree back to 1560, suspended so that moving air makes the slides gently chime against one another.

That installation, Bloodlines, is the emotional center of the show — genealogy turned into both a visual field and a soft, ambient soundscape, memory made audible. A companion piece, Left Overs (Sono stata uui), sets a table with hand-painted ceramics referencing his great-grandmother's floral motifs and embroidered napkins bearing his grandmother's phrase "I was here," treating domestic labor itself as an archive worth preserving.

The show's anchor series, LONG HAUL (i'm only crying on...), takes its title from the specific psychic space of air travel — jetlagged, anonymous, suspended between departure and arrival — and uses it as a metaphor for a life spent between countries and identities. It's a dense, personal body of work from an artist still early in his exhibition history, shown in an intimate gallery space that suits its confessional scale.

shows.title: Madonna: The Rise of the Material Girl (1980–1985)
shows.description:
Before "Madonna" meant stadium tours and reinvention as a career strategy, it meant a downtown New York dancer-turned-singer who insisted on writing her own songs and building her own image from the ground up. This photography show pulls together seven photographers — Deborah Feingold, Gary Heery, Jack Lue, Marc Canter, Mark Weiss, Mick Rock, and Richard Corman — who were in the room during those first five years, from club gigs and cassette-tape hustling to the arena-scale Like a Virgin tour of 1985.

What comes through across the prints is less a chronicle of stardom than a document of instinct: Madonna turning down a packaged pop career in Paris to keep creative control, bringing demos straight to New York DJs instead of waiting for a label, and treating her collaborators — photographers, stylists, dancers — as co-authors of a visual identity rather than hired help. Feingold's and Rock's early portraits catch her still becoming that persona in real time, all lace and attitude and un-self-conscious ambition, while Canter's tour photographs from the Universal Amphitheatre show the finished performer arriving.

Musichead Gallery, a Sunset Boulevard fixture built around rock-and-roll photography, timed the show to Madonna's new album and her first partnership with Grindr — proof, as the gallery's curator puts it, that the risk-taking on display in these early pictures never really stopped. For anyone who thinks of Madonna as pure spectacle, this is a useful corrective: a look at the specific, unglamorous decisions that built the spectacle in the first place.

shows.title: The Development Center: A Clownache Store
shows.description:
For ten days, NOON Projects hands its Chinatown storefront over to Alex Chaves and lets him blur every line between gallery, studio, and shop. The Development Center is a working outpost of Clownache, Chaves's ongoing direct-to-consumer curatorial project that mixes painting with fashion and merchandise, and for the run of the show Chaves is in residence, painting a mural on-site drawn from the geometric, low-slung architecture of early modern Los Angeles.

Alongside the mural, the space fills with new watercolors and a run of hand-produced T-shirts and editions, priced and displayed like retail goods rather than precious objects behind glass. That flattening of gallery hierarchy is very much the point: Chaves treats a hand-painted tee and a framed watercolor as equally legitimate carriers of an idea, and the installation's constant state of in-progress-ness — wet paint, a working easel, product on tables — makes the whole space feel like a stage set for the artist's process rather than a finished exhibition.

It's a small, quick-turnaround show on Chung King Road, the historic strip of storefront galleries in Chinatown that has long served as an incubator for exactly this kind of scrappy, hybrid programming, and it rewards a visit precisely because it won't look the same from one day to the next.

shows.title: f8 Group Photography Show
shows.artist: Cyndi Bemel, Steve Hymon, Richard Johnston, Dennis Lee, Krishna Malhotra, Jim Staub, and Bill Wishner
shows.description:
Once a week for nearly two decades, a small circle of photographers has been meeting in Pasadena to talk seriously about pictures — not just their own, but the history of the medium generally, from old masters to whoever the group happens to invite that week. This show is the public face of that private habit: seven members of the f8 Pasadena Salon, founded by Bill Wishner in 2007, presenting a cross-section of what nearly twenty years of close looking has produced.

Because the show comes out of a discussion group rather than a single curatorial premise, it reads less like a thesis and more like a conversation captured mid-sentence — different photographic sensibilities and subjects sitting side by side, unified mainly by a shared seriousness about craft. It's the kind of show that rewards slow looking, less about any single knockout image than the cumulative sense of a community that has spent years teaching each other how to see.

LA Artcore has operated as a scrappy, community-minded nonprofit in Little Tokyo since 1979, and a photo salon show like this one is squarely in its wheelhouse: modest, unglamorous, and genuinely rooted in the city's amateur and semi-professional art ecosystem rather than its market.

venue.name: LA Artcore Union Center for the Arts

shows.title: Trophies
shows.description:
David Hicks makes ceramics that look like they've been through something. For his third solo show with Diane Rosenstein, the Central Valley-based sculptor fills the gallery with hand-built earthenware bowls, bottles, jars, and ewers whose surfaces have been pushed through repeated firings until the glazes crack, run, and pool like weather damage. He calls the results "trophies" — not in the triumphant sense but as reliquaries for agricultural and floral cuttings, the discarded plant matter of Central California's farmland that most people never think twice about.

There's a deliberate friction in the work between the classical vessel forms Hicks builds and the chaos he then invites onto their surfaces. Titles like Sun Bleached, Red Leaf, and Marigold and Strawberries point to specific botanical sources, but the vessels themselves read as abstract fields of color and rupture — glazes in what Hicks describes as a state of "optimal softening," caught mid-collapse. The effect sits somewhere between still life and geological record.

Hicks has spent his career working at the edges of the decorative and the conceptual, and Trophies continues that project by dignifying the overlooked: agricultural byproduct, roadside scrub, the stuff that gets mowed down without ceremony. Seeing a full room of these vessels together, glazed in wildly different palettes but united by that same cracked, sun-worn surface, makes the case for paying attention to what usually gets discarded.

shows.title: Building an Audience
shows.description:
Brad Eberhard makes paintings and ceramic sculptures that feel like pages torn from a private notebook. His works are small in scale but dense with incident — shapes and colors that hover somewhere between abstraction and figuration, built up intuitively until fragments of the recognizable start to surface. For this show, he's gone a step further than usual by hand-building the frames themselves, so that a painting and the object holding it arrive as a single, inseparable decision rather than an artwork plus its display.

The imagery draws from an eclectic private archive: record-collecting, sporting geometry, archaeology, folklore, his son's patterned shirts. Eberhard has spoken about his fascination with Matisse's The Red Studio and its collapse of pictorial space, and about aspiring to the coded symbolism of Jasper Johns and the mystical smudge of Cy Twombly — lofty reference points he treats with a healthy dose of self-aware humor. The ceramic pieces, sagger-fired and glazed, extend the same sensibility into three dimensions, turning everyday objects like sconces into small, strange totems.

What ties the show together is the question posed by its title: can art exist without someone there to receive it? Eberhard's answer seems to be that the making itself is already a form of reaching out, an "oblique diary" that only completes itself in the act of being looked at. It's an intimate, unpretentious show from an artist who clearly enjoys the mechanics of painting as much as its meaning.

shows.title: Through the Sun
shows.description:
Shaghayegh Cyrous builds immersive video and sound installations out of Persian mythology, treating ancient stories as living material rather than historical decoration. Through the Sun draws its structure from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh — the medieval Persian epic — pulling on the story of Siavash, who walks through fire to prove his innocence, and Rostam's trials in the Haft Khan, to build a meditation on passage, endurance, and transformation. Fire and light become recurring thresholds throughout the work: forces that test, reveal, and ultimately renew whoever moves through them.

The show's centerpiece is Bagh (The Garden), a collaged video and sound work combining original and archival footage, staged within the gallery as a theatrical, dreamlike environment rather than a straightforward screening. Cyrous, who trained in Tehran and later earned an MFA in Social Practice at California College of the Arts, has built a career translating inherited myth and oral tradition into contemporary, often site-specific installations — her work has appeared everywhere from Tehran's MOCA to the British Museum to billboards around Los Angeles.

What makes Through the Sun land is its refusal to treat Zoroastrian cosmology and Persian epic poetry as museum-piece antiquity. Cyrous treats the search for light as both a cosmic drama and a deeply personal one, shaped as much by contemporary political and geopolitical pressure as by ancient text. The show runs concurrently with a companion presentation, Breathe the Sun, at Telematic Media Arts in San Francisco.
